newsitem.title: UK: Barratt denies UK house market overheating.
newsitem.headline: Barratt denies UK house market overheating.

text.p: British housebuilder Barratt Developments Plc said on Wednesday that reports of soaring house prices in London and the southeast had greatly exaggerated the overall state of the market.
Chairman Sir Lawrie Barratt said he believed that prices went up by about 10 percent in London last year and by about five percent in the southeast, he said.
But he said average prices nationwide went up only by about four percent, not the 8-1/2 percent suggested by some home loan providers recently, he said.
"We don't accept that and we don't accept it for this year," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We think that house price increases thoughout the country generally will be in line with increases in (people's) earnings," he said.

"That is sustainable and anything above that is not sustainable. Earnings are running at between four and five percent; if earnings continue to run at between four and five then that will be our projection for increased house prices."
Earlier the company announced a 30 percent rise in half-year profits to 24.8 million pounds before tax, on sales up 12 percent at 311.2 million pounds.
The interim dividend was increased to three pence, compared with 2.75 pence a year ago, covered by earnings of seven pence a share.

The most marked improvement in the market was in London and the southeast but "the more buoyant conditions in southern England are now gradually spreading," the chairman said in his results statement.

He also did not believe that housebuyers would be put off by an increase in borrowing rates after the government election on May 1. Interest rates were likely to go up whichever political party was in power, he said, but even a rise of one percentage point was affordable.
"Mortgage costs today are still only about seven percent," he said. "One percent would be small in the context of average mortgage costs over the past decade, of around 10-1/2 to 11 percent."

But he cautioned that a 21 percent increase in sales so far this year was in part due to Barratt's increased market share, following a regional expansion funded by a 90 million pounds rights issue made 12 months ago.

"We don't expect to continue that rate right through the year," he told Reuters. "It would run ahead of our projected expansion plan to achieve 11,000 houses a year by the year 2000 which calls for an increase of 12 percent a year."
The company had net cash at the end of 1996 of 15.8 million pounds, against net debt of 60.9 milion pounds a year ago and shareholders funds of 340.8 million pounds.

Barratt said he expected the national newbuild market to increase from 146,000 homes last year to 155,000 this year. The company increased its own build rate by 12 percent to 3,362 completions in the last half-year.
The company's land bank had been increased by 13 percent to 21,000 plots in the last year to accomodate the expansion, to sustain the company's policy of holiding land for about 30 months work.
"We are comfortable with that level," Barratt said. "That is why we have one of the best returns on capital in the industry," he added.
"There are companies who run four and five-year land banks but their return on capital can fall to about 15 percent, where our return is in excess of 20 percent."

Barratt said that land purchase costs in the last six months accounted for 23.8 percent of projected house selling prices, despite over half the acquisitions being made in the relatively expensive southeast region.
"This augurs well for future profitability," he said.
-- Greg Mahlich, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
